entry.title: The Third Scale Encoding is Hopepfully the Charm
entry.content:
Well, unfortunately time has run out, and I am not going to make the NaNoWriMo writing goal! I’m off to Japan on Monday and promised my wife that I’d do at least a little thinking about the trip before we head off. So that means I’m putting a (temporary) close on the music stuff for a few weeks. But don’t worry; I can’t get this stuff off my brain, so some time off is likely only going to stoke the flames.

With that being said…

My plan today was to write about vertical configurations and voice leadings. But I realized my notion of voice leadings didn’t agree with Tymoczko’s. And while there are a lot of music theorists whose opinions I don’t put much stock into, Tymoczko is one whose thoughts I value very much.

While trying to answer those questions, I looked at my implementation of Neo-Riemannian transformations and realized it was convoluted as all hell (which I knew). Furthermore I noticed that our work on scales the other day did almost everything I was doing by hand in the Neo-Riemannian case. So I swapped out the bespoke stuff for everyday scale things, and the tests stayed green.

Happy days. But then I changed my test generators (so that notes would include generalized accidentals) and the tests went red! For reasons unrelated to Neo-Riemannian transformations, but for darker, scarier reasons. Scales were doing the wrong thing.

Oh man. Not so good. The problem is that under our previous encoding, not all scales are retractable. Check it out:

We previously left Scales defined thusly:

type Scale :: Nat -> Nat -> Type
newtype Scale m n = Scale (Fin m -> Note n)

The codomain being Note n was so that we had a place to stick a scale degree and an accidental. We really only wanted to store a pitch class and an accidental, but you could rotate the pitch classes in a scale and then the lower pitch classes might only be reachable an octave up. Thus the degrees.

OK fine. But look at this mapping:

weird :: Scale 2 7
weird = Scale $ \case
  0 -> 0
  1 -> stepIn @12 1 0

Here we’ve defined a scale that maps both pitch classes in Fin 2 to 0 :: Deg 7, but the second pitch class also carries a (chromatic) sharp. All is well and good, until we go to invert this thing. Inverting the image of the first pitch class is fine:

let weirder = invertScaleAbove weird

applyScale weirder (0 :: Note 7)
    == (0 :: Deg 2)

but inverting the image of the second, well…

applyScale weirder (stepIn @12 1 0 :: Note 7)
    == stepIn @12 1 0 :: Deg 2

Because application of scales dispatches only on pitch classes, it can’t branch on the accidental here. So what was once in the image of weird is now somehow getting smuggled along when we apply the inverse of weird. Weird!

This is a fundamental problem with our scales as written. They simply do not always admit left inverses!

To be clear, the problem here is that weird isn’t injective in its mappings from Fin 2 to Fin 7 (both 0, 1 :: Fin 2 end up at 0 :: Fin 7.) So if we could force the scale to be injective, then the error conditions wouldn’t apply, and we always would be able to find a left inverse.

So then, how do we ensure we have an injective mapping between finite numbers?

A Quick Musical Note

As an aside to the main thrust of this blog post, I found it quite elucidating to think about what this “injective mapping of pitch classes” constraint actually means in terms of music.

And I THINK that this is the underlying constraint that enharmonic spelling is attempting to solve.

Recall that the standard musical staff notates the diatonic scale (Fin 7), which corresponds (roughly) to the white keys on the piano. For time immemorial we have been working in Fin 7, and this is why the black keys don’t have their own names – because the black keys are the five notes that you need to add in to get to Fin 12. We happily talk about the white notes as A, B, C, D, E, F, G, but the black notes are relegated to mere modifiers — sometimes as D#, other times as Eb. But never as DE.

Anyway, since we can’t call it the note between D and E as DE, what can we do? Well we need to project this note down to Fin 7. Which of course can’t be done in general, but we cheat by adding an accidental. Is it either D# or Eb? It depends! What does it depend on?

Conventional spelling rules say that it ought to be offset from “the scale note it is acting in place of.” Which is to say that it must be temporarily replacing some note in the scale, and it steals that note’s pitch class!

If we pull this back to injective mapping of finite numbers, the weird historical rule makes sense. In order to preserve this injective mapping you must remove any other notes which would otherwise map to the same pitch class!

I feel like I am not articulating this very well. Maybe some diagrams would help. But I’d actually like to go to bed sometime tonight and there is still too much to write down before I need to put the book ends on my music project for a few weeks. Alas.

Let me know in the comments if any of this section makes a lick of sense. Or if it doesn’t. That’s what we call e n g a g e m e n t, baby.

Dependently-Typed Programming to the Rescue

OK so anyway, back to trying to enforce injectivity of finite maps.

Thankfully I wrote a book on Agda which happens to be pretty helpful for working out solutions to stuff like this.

Recall that functions Fin n -> a are isomorphic to vectors Vec n a (which is to say, a product of n copies of a.) This fact will come up again when I eventually get around to writing about voice leadings. But you will notice that functions Fin n -> a are not injective functions between Fins!

To be concrete, let’s say we’re looking for mappings of the form Fin m -> (Fin n, a). Which solves our scale problem (because we can put our accidentals in a.) So as a first step, we could consider encoding this mapping as:

Vec m (Maybe a)

with the invariant that there be exactly n elements that contain as. For example, triad :: Scale 3 7 would look like this:

triad' :: Vec 7 (Maybe (Accidentals Int))
triad' = let a = mempty
  in Just a
  :> Nothing
  :> Just a
  :> Nothing
  :> Just a
  :> Nothing
  :> Nothing
  :> Nil

Here we have filled exactly 3 of the 7 total slots. We can then recover the mapping by traversing over the Justs and pairing each with the next Fin 3:

triad'' :: Vec 7 (Maybe (Fin 3, Accidentals Int))
triad'' = let a = mempty
  in Just (0, a)
  :> Nothing
  :> Just (1, a)
  :> Nothing
  :> Just (2, a)
  :> Nothing
  :> Nothing
  :> Nil

Now if we zip this vector with its own indices, we get this:

triad''' :: Vec 7 (Fin 7, Maybe (Fin 3, Accidentals Int))
triad''' = let a = mempty
  in (0, Just (0, a))
  :> (1, Nothing)
  :> (2, Just (1, a))
  :> (3, Nothing)
  :> (4, Just (2, a))
  :> (5, Nothing)
  :> (6, Nothing)
  :> Nil

Finally, filter out the Nothings, and you’re left with (he said, gesticulating wildly) exactly three values, and their corresponding indices in both Fin 3 and Fin 7:

triad'''' :: [(Fin 7, (Fin 3, Accidentals Int))]
triad'''' = let a = mempty
  in [ (0, (0, a))
     , (2, (1, a))
     , (4, (2, a))
     ]

Since you and I both “know” that there are three elements in this list, we can give a “total” function:

triad :: Fin 3 -> (Fin 7, Accidentals Int)
triad n = triad'''' !! fromIntegral n

Sure enough this does work! But it only works because of our invariant that there are exactly1 3 Justs in our original vector. That’s cool and all, but it seems like the sort of thing that would be easy to get wrong. And then you’d be crashing at runtime, and that’s not the Haskell Ethos.

So what can we do instead? Let’s make a type that is like a Vec, but which counts slots separately from filled slots. I needed a name so I called it an MVec, but the M doesn’t actually stand for anything. Behold:

type MVec :: Nat -> Nat -> Type -> Type
data MVec slots filled a where
  MNil ::                              MVec  0           0           a
  MCons :: a -> MVec slots filled a -> MVec (slots + 1) (filled + 1) a
  MSkip ::      MVec slots filled a -> MVec (slots + 1)  filled      a

Here, MCons acts exactly like :> did in our vector example — it sticks an element in front of another MVec. But in doing so, it increases the slots and the fill count both by one. However, there’s also MSkip which only increases the slots (and correspondingly doesn’t have a place to put an a.)

This structure thus perfectly encodes our m slots of which exactly n are filled semantics. Very cool. As a little proof, we can project a MVec m n a down to either a Vec n a or a Vec m (Maybe a):

embedMVec :: MVec m n a -> Vec n a
embedMVec MNil = Nil
embedMVec (MCons a as) = a :> embedMVec as
embedMVec (MSkip as) = embedMVec as

projectMVec :: MVec m n a -> Vec m (Maybe a)
projectMVec MNil = Nil
projectMVec (MCons a as) = Just a :> projectMVec as
projectMVec (MSkip as) = Nothing :> projectMVec as

So that’s all well and good. But we can also actually find things in this data structure, as given by mlookup:

mlookup :: MVec m n a -> Fin n -> (Fin m, a)
mlookup (MCons a _) FZ = (FZ, a)
mlookup (MCons _ mn) (FS n) =
  case mlookup mn n of
    (m, a) -> (FS m, a)
mlookup (MSkip mn) n =
  case mlookup mn n of
    (m, a) -> (FS m, a)

which you will happily note follows the same logic we worked through for triad, and is exactly the function we want to use for making Scales.

We can also go the other way, and search on the Fin m indices:

msearch :: MVec m n a -> Fin m -> Maybe (Fin n, a)
msearch MNil a = case a of
msearch (MCons a _) FZ = Just (FZ, a)
msearch (MCons _ as) (FS n) = fmap (first FS) $ msearch as n
msearch (MSkip _) FZ = Nothing
msearch (MSkip as) (FS n) = msearch as n

which I’m not super sure is important, but it was fun to write.

The real reason for calling this thing MVec was so that I could put ms in front of all its functions’ names. Which finally pays off when we get to the MVec composition function:

malign
  :: (x -> y -> z)
  -> MVec c b x
  -> MVec b a y
  -> MVec c a z
malign _ MNil MNil = MNil
malign f (MSkip bc) ab = MSkip $ malign f bc ab
malign f (MCons x bc) (MCons y ab) = MCons (f x y) $ malign f bc ab
malign f (MCons _ bc) (MSkip ab) = MSkip $ malign f bc ab

This function does end-wise composition of MVecs. If you have one MVec that has c slots and b items, and another which has b slots and a items (sorry for the type variable shuffling!), then we ought to be able to make an MVec with c slots and only a items. This corresponds to composition of scales, so it’s really quite important!

The trick is we traverse over the b-in-c collection. Whenever we find an item there, we consider it to be a potential slot of the a-in-b collection. If a-in-b says to skip, then we skip it. But if they’re both cons cells, we can use the given function to combine their values into a z.

Quite nice if you ask me.

Back To Scales

Now that we have MVecs, it’s pretty trivial to implement the small-to-big scale mapping that we’ve been thinking about. Really we just need to keep an MVec m n around, convert it into the old representation via mlookup, and then all of the last post’s machinery around scales works just fine.

Except, how do you invert them? Remember that we did all of this work to invert them. If an MVec m n has m slots of which n are full, it necessarily means that n <= m. Which is to say that it’s slightly more complicated than just keeping a MVec m n around.

The trick of course is that if you invert a scale, it’s still the same MVec you need! Thus a Scale a b is either an embedding from a to b, or a projection from b back to a:

type Scale :: Nat -> Nat -> Type
data Scale a b where
  Embed   ::                 MVec b a (Accidentals Int) -> Scale a b
  Project :: Quantization -> MVec b a (Accidentals Int) -> Scale b a

Notice that it’s the same MVec in both constructors, the only difference is which direction the scale goes. This Quantization thing is a little enum:

data Quantization = Below | Above | Nearest

which corresponds exactly to the three invertScale* functions from last time. Really it means “if you’re looking at a scale degree which doesn’t fit, which note should we add offsets to?” I don’t think I like having this field, and when I’m back from Japan I’ll explore just sticking the chooser in there.

Once we’ve added Project, however, I don’t think scales compose anymore. Not to fear, we’ll just make them compose by adding a new constructor:

data Scale a b where
  Embed   ::                 MVec b a (Accidentals Int) -> Scale a b
  Project :: Quantization -> MVec b a (Accidentals Int) -> Scale b a
  Compose :: Scale x b -> Scale a x                     -> Scale a b

Composition of scales tries to malign when possible:

compScale :: Scale b c -> Scale a b -> Scale a c
compScale (Embed bc) (Embed ab) = Embed $ malign (<>) bc ab
compScale bc ab = Compose bc ab

and inversion is now a little swap-er-oo of our constructors:

invertScale :: Quantization -> Scale a b -> Scale b a
invertScale q (Embed slots) = Project q slots
invertScale _ (Project _ slots) = Embed slots
invertScale q (Compose f g) = Compose (invertScale q g) (invertScale q f)

So that’s the thrust of today’s work. Having sorted out all of these details has dramatically simplified up the codebase (and found a bunch of bugs), which I always consider to be a harbinger of being on the right track. Making any of this stuff usable is its own exercise in existential types and type reflection shenanigans, but maybe we’ll cover that another day if there’s sufficient interest.

entry.title: Generalized Accidentals
entry.content:
Just a little note on yesterday’s ornamental offsets. I realized overnight that this idea is way less weird to musicians than originally thought. The offset idea is really just generalized accidentals.

Check it out: standard music notation, without ever saying so, assumes a Fin 7 scale. The notation maps these degrees alternatingly between lines and spaces-between-lines. Thus 0..6 :: Deg 7 look like this:

which correspond to seven contiguous white keys on the piano. But the piano also has five black keys between any seven contiguous white keys. Adding in the black keys gets us an additional five pitch classes, which brings us up to the Fin 12 scale that Western music is based around.

Modulo some technicalities, there’s no way to notate these black keys directly. The black key between C and D is known either as “C sharp” or “D flat” — sharps moving one offset up in Deg 12, and flats moving one offset down. Thus the twelve pitch classes of the chromatic scale are notated either as sharps:

or equivalently, as flats:

Although it is usually omitted, there is also a “natural” symbol, to indicate the absence of a sharp or a flat. If we include these symbols into our sharps example, we get this:

which represents exactly the same thing as the “Chromatic Sharps” figure. We’re just being a little more pedantic here.

To drive everything home, these accidental symbols are exactly the Deg 12 ornaments on a Note 7 that we were investigating last time. If we change the ♮ symbol to 0, the ♯ to +1 and the ♭ to -1, our chromatic scales look like this:

Both examples now have “obvious” encodings as Note 7s: use the notated pitch as the Deg 7, and the offset as a stepIn @12. Thus “Explicit Accidental Sharps” is encoded as:

[ 0
, stepIn @12 1 0
, 1
, stepIn @12 1 1
, 2
, 3
, stepIn @12 1 3
, 4
, stepIn @12 1 4
, 5
, stepIn @12 1 5
, 6
] :: [Note 7]

Rather unsurprisingly, when we applyScale diatonic over this collection, we get [0..11] :: Note 12, which is just to say that this enumerates all of the pitch classes in the chromatic scale. And of course it does, because we designed it that way in the first place!

So this all brings us back to yesterday’s Ornaments type, which allows us to express offsets at any scale degree — not just Deg 12 like sharps and flats in standard musical notation allow us to target. So let’s broaden our visualization a little more, making it explicit that our chromatic offsets are in Deg 12:

Now that this has been made explicit, there’s no reason why we can’t add multiple accidentals to any given note. For example, we could make put a stepIn @10 2 on the second note, in addition to a stepsIn @12 (-1)!

This one says that if we were to map our Note 7 into Note 10, we’d move the second note up by 2 :: Deg 10. Then when we mapped the resulting Note 10s into Note 12, we’d move that note again — this time down by -1 :: Deg 12.

So the ideas here really are familiar to musicians — the standard notation just makes it hard to see what it is we’re talking about.

To give a bit more of a musical example, we can give a little triadic motif:

Notice that the third note here is one Deg 7 above the Note 3, while the fourth note is one Deg 12 below the Note 3. In musical terms, we’re arpeggiating a triad, but inserting a diatonic note above the “third” and a chromatic note below the “fifth” (scare quotes because the thirds and fifths move!)

If we then repeat this motif twice more, each time one Deg 3 up, we get this:

Finally, mapping this sequence into standard notation (assuming we map via triad and diatonic) produces this rather pleasing melody:

Notice how what was a completely regular pattern in Note 3 expands out unevenly each time around, producing interesting motific development.

Hopefully this gives a taste of what all that Note and Ornaments nonsense from yesterday is all about. Not only are these ideas already familiar to musicians, they also immediately produce musically interesting results!

entry.title: Musical Notes and Scales
entry.content:
Sorry for the delay. Everyone in my household came down with egregious sicknesses. And I had a bunch of unsatisfying things in my music theory that needed to get worked out. But we’re mostly better and the theoretical issues are resolved, so we’re BACK baby.

Over the last two posts we discussed abstract musical pitches and (some) efficient voice leadings which help move us smoothly between different configurations in musical space.

It’s been all very interesting musically, but you must admit there hasn’t been much in the way of functional programming going on. Today we’re going to get back to brass tacks and see about making all of these notions precise, compositional, and fun to work with.

Where we left things is with a Fin n type:

type Fin :: Nat -> Type
data Fin n

instance  KnownNat n          => Enum    (Fin n)
instance (KnownNat n, 1 <= n) => Bounded (Fin n)

which has exactly n distinct values. We then made a Deg n type, whose semantics are “exactly one of n distinct values, with an octave component.” We represent this implicitly by way of an Int:

type Deg :: Nat -> Type
newtype Deg n = Deg
  { getDeg :: Int
  }
  deriving stock (Generic)
  deriving newtype (Eq, Ord, Show, Num, Enum, Real, Integral)

and give its semantics by way of a function:

degToPC :: KnownNat n => Deg n -> (Int, Fin n)
degToPC (Deg d) =
  let (oct, pc) = divMod d n
   in (oct, toEnum pc)

where the output Int is which octave the degree ended up in.

We have then been discussing “scales” as mappings of the form Fin m -> Fin n. These have always been in scare quotes because this is not really how musicians traditionally think about scales! Whatever this mapping concept is, it doesn’t really have a standard name in musical vocabulary. But scales are the closest thing semantically, so we’re going to just shadow that name and go about our business.

It’s a bit of a tricky line to balance. So whenever we’re talking about the loose musical idea, we’ll use the word “scale.” And whenever we mean this mapping, we’ll go with Scale.

Some Failed Attempts at Pinnning Down Scales

However, it’s been a bit of a simplification to say a Scale is a mapping Fin n -> Fin m. We’d like our Scales to be monotone mappings, which is to say that if i :: Deg m <= j :: Deg m, then (applyScale sc i) :: Deg n <= (applyScale sc j) :: Deg n. Enforcing monotonicity on Fin-to-Fin mappings is possible, but it requires us to preserve the ordering of pitch classes within a single octave. That is to say, it means we can’t do any sort of permutation.

Thus, perhaps we should think about Scales as mappings Fin m -> Deg n. This is much closer to what we want (although it has some shortcomings that we will see shortly.) But let’s move forward with this attempt in order to motivate some of the later decisions:

type Scale :: Nat -> Nat -> Type
newtype Scale m n = Scale (Fin m -> Deg n)

We can introduce a new scale by way of mkScale:

mkScale :: (KnownNat m, 1 <= m) => (Fin m -> Deg n) -> Scale m n
mkScale f =
  let image = sort $ do
        m <- [0 .. maxBound @(Fin m)]
        pure $ f m
   in Scale $ \m -> image !! fromEnum m

which enumerates all values in f, sorts them (in order to ensure monotonicity), and then builds a Scale that uses the Fin m to select from the sorted values.

We can apply a scale to a Deg by way of applyScale:

applyScale
    :: forall m n
     . Scale m n
    -> Deg m
    -> Deg n
applyScale (Scale f) (Deg dm) =
  let (oct, pc) = divMod dm $ scaleSize @m
      Deg dn = f $ toEnum pc
   in Deg (dn + oct * scaleSize @n)

which ensures we preserve the necessary semantics of degToPC given earlier.

All is so far well and good. But not for long.

In some cases we might want to reverse a Scale’s mapping, eg going from Deg 7 to Deg 3. This makes a lot of sense musically. For example, we might want to include a neighbor note, or a passing tone when writing out otherwise-triadic music. More directly, projecting down to a smaller abstract pitch class is the exact mechanism of tintinnabuli.

Unfortunately however, reversing a mapping Fin m -> Deg n is obvious hogwash from the perspective of our functional programming ivory tower. In the usual case that m <= n, this is a very non-injective function, so we have no chance of turning it around.

And yet, it’s musically meaningful. So, regardless of whether we can do it in Haskell, we somehow must. Otherwise whatever it is we’ve built is modeling the wrong thing.

Our mental pattern matchers that say “you can’t reverse a non-bijective function” are absolutely correct. But it’s worth taking a moment to think about why exactly we can’t in this case. Consider the musically-common case of working in a Scale 3 7 = Fin 3 -> Deg 7. Here, some of the Deg 7s are targeted by the Fin 3. In particular, 0, 2, 4 :: Deg 7 get targeted by the triad scale introduced in a previous post.

So reversing 0, 2, 4 :: Fin 7 is easy enough — we just send them to 0, 1, 2 :: Deg 3. The hard part is deciding where ought we send 1, 3, 5, 6 :: Fin 7. Well, why don’t we just send them to themselves?

Sounds a little crazy, I know, but check this out. If we could attach other scalar degree offsets to each note, we could invert a scale by mapping the image directly to the domain whenever possible. And when it’s not possible, we could represent it as an offset from the nearest thing in the domain.

A little example might help. Say we have 0..7 :: Fin 7 and we’d like to reverse them across a Scale 3 7. If we represent exact points in Deg 3 as white note heads, and “offsets” as black note heads, one possible reverse mapping looks like this:

If we assume we have some operation (/+) :: Fin 3 -> Deg 7 -> Note 3, this diagram corresponds to:

[0, 0 /+ 1, 1, 1 /+ 1, 2, 2 /+ 1, 2 /+ 2, 3]

Of course, such a mapping is not unique. For example, we can also do a “round up, offset down” approach:

which is similarly:

[0, 1 /- 1, 1, 2 /- 1, 2, 3 /- 2, 3 /- 1, 3]

All of this is to say that Degs aren’t quite what we’re looking for!

Enter Notes

As we’ve seen, Degs aren’t quite powerful enough to represent these offsets. So we’ll first need to make a type to hold the offsets. The closest standard-musical terminology here is “ornamentation,” so that’s what we’ll go with.

An Ornaments is a mapping from scalar sizes to offsets. Rather than keeping the scalar sizes around in the type system (as we have done for Fin and Deg and Scale), here we’re going to simplify things down to an IntMap:

newtype Ornaments a = Ornaments
  { getOrnaments :: IntMap a
  }
  deriving stock (Generic, Functor)
  deriving newtype (Show)
  deriving (Semigroup, Monoid) via MonoidalIntMap (Sum a)

Two Ornaments are equal when they have the same non-zero elements:

normalizeOrnaments :: (Num a, Eq a) => Ornaments a -> Ornaments a
normalizeOrnaments = Ornaments . IM.filter (/= 0) . getOrnaments

instance (Eq a, Num a) => Eq (Ornaments a) where
  (==) = on (==) (getOrnaments . normalizeOrnaments)

instance (Ord a, Num a) => Ord (Ornaments a) where
  compare = on compare (getOrnaments . normalizeOrnaments)

We can also introduce Ornaments:

ornament :: forall n a. KnownNat n => a -> Ornaments a
ornament = Ornaments . IM.singleton (scaleSize @n)

and eliminate them:

decompOrnament
    :: forall n
     . KnownNat n
    => Ornaments Int
    -> (Ornaments Int, Deg n)
decompOrnament o
  = maybe
      (o, 0)
      ( (coerce (IM.filterWithKey @Int (\k _ -> k /= scaleSize @n)) o, )
      . Deg
      )
  $ IM.lookup (scaleSize @n)
  $ getOrnaments o

getOrnament :: forall n. KnownNat n => Ornaments Int -> Deg n
getOrnament = snd . decompOrnament

Here decompOrnament @n returns the Deg n ornament, and returns a new Ornaments with that scale degree removed. If you don’t care about the removal, you’re welcome to call getOrnament directly.

Armed with Ornaments, we can now make Note, which wraps a degree with ornaments:

type Note :: Nat -> Type
data Note n = Note (Deg n) (Ornaments Int)
  deriving stock (Generic, Eq, Ord)

Notes admit a Num instance, which combines ornaments pointwise:

instance Num (Note n) where
  fromInteger n = Note (fromInteger n) mempty
  Note a as + Note b bs = Note (a + b) $ as <> bs
  Note a as - Note b bs = Note (a - b) $ as <> fmap negate bs
  Note a (Ornaments as) * Note b (Ornaments bs) =
    Note (a * b) $ Ornaments $ IM.intersectionWith (*) as bs
  abs    (Note a as) = Note (abs a)    $ fmap abs    as
  signum (Note a as) = Note (signum a) $ fmap signum as

and we can add an ornamental offset to a Note by way of stepIn @c:

stepIn :: forall c n. (KnownNat c, KnownNat n) => Int -> Note n -> Note n
stepIn k (Note a as) =
  case scaleSize @c == scaleSize @n of
    True -> Note (a + Deg k) as
    False -> Note a $ as <> ornament @c k

An invariant enforced by stepIn is that you never have an ornament of size n attached to a note also of size n. If you attempt to, we just change the Deg n instead.

Scales Revisited

Now that we have Notes, we can define Scales in terms of them, and we are rewarded with a convenient place to stick offsets when we invert scales. Scale and mkScale change only in that we reference Note instead of Deg:

type Scale :: Nat -> Nat -> Type
newtype Scale m n = Scale (Fin m -> Note n)
mkScale :: (KnownNat m, 1 <= m) => (Fin m -> Note n) -> Scale m n
mkScale f =
  let image = sort $ do
        m <- [0 .. maxBound @(Fin m)]
        pure $ f m
   in Scale $ \m -> image !! fromEnum m

However, applyScale needs to do slightly more work: it must respect incoming and outgoing ornamentation. The Note m might have a n-sized ornament, in which case we must add it immediately. And then we must combine the remaining ornaments with any which might arise from the Scale’s mapping:

applyScale
    :: forall m n
     . Scale m n
    -> Note m
    -> Note n
applyScale (Scale f) (Note (Deg dm) os) =
  let (oct, pc) = divMod dm $ scaleSize @m
      (Note (Deg dn) os') = f $ toEnum pc
      (os'', od) = decompOrnament @n os
   in Note (od + Deg (dn + oct * scaleSize @n)) $ os' <> os''

With all of this work, we’re now ready to tackle inverting scales. The thrust of the idea here is a relatively simple algorithm:

  1. Compute the image of the scale. Take the resulting pitch class, and associate it with the corresponding input pitch class. Negate the octave and ornaments when doing this.
  2. Check if the inverse pitch class exist directly in your image map. If so, return it directly.
  3. If not, select the best candidate of the image with respect to the inverse pitch class. Compute how far the best candidate is away from the input, and add that distance as an extra ornament.

Of course, the devil is in the details. Getting the “best candidate” might require looking in a different octave. We wrap the candidate logic into a chooser:

(forall x. Ord x => Fin b -> [(Fin b, x)] -> (Int, x))

which receives the desired pitch class, the image, and must return one element of the image along with an octave displacement. Since the entire thing is stuck in a forall x, the chooser is allowed only to look at the Fin bs to determine what is the best candidate. As a little illustration here, we might want to round up to the nearest pitch class in the image. So we’d want to filter the image by anything >= pc. But if pc is already the largest thing in the image, we’d instead want to return the smallest thing in the image with a +1 octave offset.

If you’re curious, the logic in its full glory is thus:

invertScale
    :: forall a b
     . (1 <= a)
    => (forall x. Ord x => Fin b -> [(Fin b, x)] -> (Int, x))
    -> Scale a b
    -> Scale b a
invertScale choose (Scale f) = do
  let img :: [(Fin b, Note a)]
      img = do
        a <- [0 .. maxBound @(Fin a)]
        let (Note (Deg db) os) = f a
        let (o, pc) = divMod db $ scaleSize @b
        let b = toEnum @(Fin b) pc
        pure ( b
             , Note (fromIntegral a - Deg (scaleSize @a * o))
                 $ fmap negate os
             )
  Scale $ \b ->
    case lookup b img of
      Just a -> a
      Nothing -> do
        let (ox, chosen) = choose b img
            (b', Note da os) =
              case find ((== chosen) . snd) img of
                Just c -> c
                Nothing -> error "impossible"
            diff = fromIntegral b - (fromIntegral b' + ox * scaleSize @b)
        Note (da + Deg (ox * scaleSize @a)) $ os <> ornament @b diff

which we specialize with a few different choices of chooser:

invertScaleAbove   :: (1 <= a) => Scale a b -> Scale b a
invertScaleBelow   :: (1 <= a) => Scale a b -> Scale b a
invertScaleNearest :: (1 <= a) => Scale a b -> Scale b a

As a little aside, I haven’t found a great way of naming the first two functions. Here “above” means “round down and offset up”, and below is the opposite. Any suggestions for more obvious names here would be greatly appreciated.

That’s all for today. In the next post we’ll investigate the types behind voice leadings, with a similar attention to precision.

entry.title: Voice Leadings on Abstract Musical Pitches
entry.content:
In the last post, we discussed the notion of abstract musical pitches. I was writing that under a haze of covid-inspired single-parenting, so we’re going to take a few more minutes to try to clarify some of the claims made in that one, before moving on to doing more interesting things with the concept.

In Haskell we have this function quotRem :: Integral a => a -> a -> (a, a), which computes the quotient and remainder of one number divided by another. For example, quotRem 25 5 == (5, 0), quotRem 25 6 == (4, 1), quotRem 25 7 == (3, 4). You get the picture.

Our Deg n type from yesterday operates over quotRem _ n. That is, any degree we might have, say k :: Deg n, we compute its quotRem k n to get (octave, pitchClass). This motivates why we were using functions Fin n -> Fin m to model “scales” mapping from Deg n into Deg m — we want to map only the pitchClass part of the quotRem.

To be more precise, if we want to map a Deg n into Deg m, we run this function:

scale :: (Fin n -> Fin m) -> Deg n -> Deg m
scale f (Deg dn) =
  let (oct, pc) = quotRem dn n
   in Deg $ fromEnum (f (toEnum pc)) + oct * m

This mapping only of pitch classes ensures we maintain the quotienting structure of Deg n that requires k + n to be the same pitch class as k.

Musically, none of this should be unfamiliar. In a diatonic scale, you have 7 distinct notes — let’s label them “do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti.” These correspond to 0, 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 :: Deg 7. If you start at any of these notes and go up (or down) 7 times, you will get back to the same pitch class an octave higher (or lower.)

The same argument works for the chromatic scale, where we have 12 notes, labeled “A, A#, B, C, C#, D, D#, E, F, F#, G, G#”. Express these as 0, 1, ..., 11 :: Deg 12, and then go up or down 12 spots and you end up back where you were, modulo an octave.

Similarly, if we want to map from the diatonic scale (Deg 7) to the chromatic scale (Deg 12), we choose 7 pitch classes from the 12 available, and respect the octave equivalence (this mapping is given implicitly by a key signature and, in notated music, a clef.)

If none of these music words make any sense to you, don’t worry. It doesn’t matter.

Intrinsic Scales

Check this out: nothing says we need to have a statically-known-at-compile-time n for our Deg n. As an illustration, here’s the beginning of the Star Wars theme:

Out of the 7 diatonic pitch classes, this segment of the theme uses only five: do, re, mi, fa, sol, la, ti. So we can project the Star Wars theme down to a 5-note clef:

and give a mapping:

starWarsScale :: Deg 5 -> Deg 7
starWarsScale 0 = 0
starWarsScale 1 = 1
starWarsScale 2 = 4
starWarsScale 3 = 5
starWarsScale 4 = 6

which, of course, when we apply that mapping back to the 5-note version, gives us back the song we started with. But before transforming it back, we can do funny things, like fmap (+ 1) in the 5-note scale:

Mapping this back to Deg 7 (and then all the way to concrete pitches) gives us this neat little take on Star Wars:

Not as good as John Williams’ to be sure, but it’s interesting that we can do this transformation!

All of this is to say that for any Foldable and Functor collection of notes, we can get its intrinsic scale via intrinsic:

intrinsic
  :: (Foldable f, Functor f)
  => f (Deg n)
  -> (forall i. (Fin i -> Fin n) -> f (Deg i) -> r)
  -> r

which is “you give me some collection of Deg ns, and I’ll give you back a collection of Deg is, as well as a scale from Fin i -> Fin n”. Where i is some unknown-at-compile-time number corresponding to however many unique pitch-classes were in your collection.

As we have seen with the Star Wars example, we can find the intrinsic scale for horizontal structures.1 But of course, this is parameterized over any Functor/Foldable type constructor f. So we can find lots of intrinsic scales — think chords and vertical structures. But probably also more things if I were more imaginative!

Efficient Voice Leadings

We are going to need a few “scales” to work with in this section. We’ll take two common mappings from Western tonal music, namely the 3-in-7 mapping (“triads”), and the 7-in-12 mapping (“the diatonic scale”.)

triad :: Fin 3 -> Fin 7
triad 0 = 0
triad 1 = 2
triad 2 = 4

diatonic :: Fin 7 -> Fin 12
diatonic 0 = 0
diatonic 1 = 2
diatonic 2 = 4
diatonic 3 = 5
diatonic 4 = 7
diatonic 5 = 9
diatonic 6 = 11

If you are not classically-trained in music, don’t worry very much about this. You’d recognize these sounds if you heard them. For example, the triad mapping sounds like any of the examples from the Wikipedia page on arpeggios. The diatonic mapping sounds like this. We’re just arbitrarily choosing some ways of mapping between our abstract degrees (in a way that happens to line up with the arbitrariness of Western musical tradition.)

In Tonality Tymoczko points out that these mappings happen to pretty evenly divide the octave. To illustrate what this means, look at triad: it maps 0..6 :: Deg 3 to 0, 2, 4, 7, 9, 11 :: Deg 7, which if you take the difference between any two subsequent degrees in the image is 2, 2, 3, 2, 2. That’s about as evenly as you could map these things! There’s a tiny little bump in the pattern going from 4 to 7.

The same thing happens in diatonic. We map 0..8 :: Deg 7 to 0, 2, 4, 5, 7, 9, 11, 12, 14 :: Deg 12, which again, taking the difference between subsequent numbers is 2, 2, 1, 2, 2, 2, 1, 2. Very evenly spaced!

Note that this doesn’t actually need to have been the case! This is a property of triad and diatonic, not of Deg {3,7,12}. And Tymoczko makes a pretty compelling argument that this property is why Western music has historically been organized around triad and diatonic.

So why is this important? It’s to do with the slight non-regularity in scale degrees. A big theme of Tonality is that we can very-nearly offset movement in Deg m with an opposite movement in Deg n, and that this is musically interesting (and ubiquitous!)

For example, when working with triad, it happens that moving up by two steps in the intrinsic scale (Deg 3) is almost exactly cancelled out by moving down five steps in the containing scale (Deg 7):

The second chord (black note-heads) here is the first one moved up by 2 :: Deg 3, while the third chord is the second one moved down by 5 :: Deg 7. As you can see, we end up almost exactly where we started, except that the bottom pitch has moved one step down.

In fact, this phenomenon happens again and again if we continue performing these moves. As before, the movement in the intrinsic scale is shown with black note-heads, while the movement in the containing scale is shown with white ones.

Sure enough, this makes pretty pictures. And if you can read the musical notation, you’ll know that what we happen to be computing here are efficient voice leadings from a root note to the diatonic third above it.

In fact, if we remove the in-between black notes, we end up with this:

which sounds like this:

This is likely the sort of thing which is pretty exciting if you’re a musician, and “who cares” if you’re not. It doesn’t really sound like music, but this is in a very real sense a fundamental building block of (Western) music. It’s a way of smoothly getting from one place to another in a musical space. Any time you don’t notice a jarring chord change, this is likely the mechanism by which the music is moving.

Modal Modulations

We can do the same move with 7-in-12 modulations. If we look at the notes of the diatonic (C major) scale as a vertical chord:

Now if we map it up by 4 scale degrees, and down by 7 chromatic degrees we end up here:

which is either C mixolydian, or a smooth voice-leading into F major, depending on how you look at it.

Making the same up 4 down 7 move again now moves us into C dorian, or Bb major, again, depending on your perspective.

Of course, I didn’t just pick the +4-7 thing out of my brain. Tymoczko has a great tool for computing the moves involved here, and it works for any sized chord inside of any sized scale.

Wrapping Up

A weird one today. Not much in the way of Haskell, and either fascinating or dead boring (depending on how much imagination you have) if you’re into the music theory. In the next post we’ll see about how to formalize all of this into first-class objects. And then we might be getting somewhat close to actually making some music. Maybe?

  1. With some finagling, granted. Those Events end up being pretty annoying to have to work around! This is a pretty good indication that everyone emailing me saying “you don’t need to model discreteness” are probably right, but I don’t actually know how to make that happen.↩︎

entry.title: Abstract Musical Pitches
entry.content:
This is my seventh blog post in a series about “solving music”, in terms of giving it a precise and useful constructive algebra. And somehow despite 10,000 words on the topic, we have yet to discuss any notion of the common musical ideas of “scales” or “harmony” or “pitches.”

Today we’re going to tackle those things

I’d like to preface this by saying: all of the music theory here comes from Dmitri Tymoczko. I’ve spent the last year reading (and rereading, and re-rereading) his amazing book Tonality which is the clearest approach to music I have ever found. Shoutouts to Dmitri Volkov who put me onto the trail.

To the extent that I’ve done anything of substance on this matter, it is merely in finding representations of these ideas in terms of types!

Finite Numbers

Let’s set the stage with a little appetizer. Consider the finite numbers:

type Fin :: Nat -> Type
data Fin n

The type Fin n has n distinct values, which we label 0, 1, …, n. For example Fin 0 has 0 values, Fin 3 has 3 values, and so on and so forth.

Encoding Fin in Haskell is tricky and rather unsatisfying regardless of how you do it. For our purposes, we’re going to do this:

type Fin :: Nat -> Type
data Fin n where
  FZ :: (1 <= n) => Fin n
  FS :: (1 <= n) => !(Fin (n - 1)) -> Fin n

which lets us encode 0 as FZ, 1 as FS FZ, etc. The funny 1 <= n constraints are there to help GHC learn that these patterns are complete. Like I said, rather unsatisfying, but what are you going to do.

The advantage of doing things this way is that when combined with ghc-typelits-natnormalise, GHC can deduce that eg isOdd is defined over all possible inputs:

isOdd :: Fin 3 -> Bool
isOdd FZ = True
isOdd (FS FZ) = False
isOdd (FS (FS FZ)) = True

We will give the following instances over Fin n:

deriving instance Eq (Fin n)
deriving instance Ord (Fin n)

instance (...) => Num (Fin n) where
  fromInteger = unsafeFromNum . flip mod (natSize @n)
  n + m = fromInteger (toInteger n + toInteger m)
  n * m = fromInteger (toInteger n * toInteger m)
  n - m = fromInteger (toInteger n - toInteger m)

where the Num instances are up to mod n. That is, (2 :: Fin 3) + 2 is equal to 1 :: Fin 3 (because 4 mod 3 is 1.) While GHC will happily allow us to use integer literals to define pattern matches against Fin n, it won’t be able to tell that they’re total. Alas. Alack. Nevertheless, for reasons of presentation we will pretend like GHC can. So we will prefer to write isOdd like this:

isOdd :: Fin 3 -> Bool
isOdd 0 = True
isOdd 1 = False
isOdd 2 = True

Scalar Degrees

Let’s talk music now.

We begin with the idea of a “scale degree”, which is just an integer acting as a coordinate in some “musical space”, to be made precise later. Our type is Deg n, where n is the size of the scale.

type Deg :: Nat -> Type
newtype Deg n = Deg
  { getDeg :: Int
  }
  deriving stock (Generic)
  deriving newtype (Eq, Ord, Show, Num, Enum, Real, Integral)

Really, we just keep the n around to ensure you don’t accidentally add Degs that belong in different coordinate systems.

However, unlike Int, we are going to do some quotienty stuff with Deg n. Namely, we will say that (k + n) :: Deg n is “the same thing, only higher” than k :: Deg n.

In musical terms, n is the number of pitch classes available to us (notes like A, B, C#, Db, etc.). And so our claim about k + n is like saying (C4 + an octave) = C5 is the “same thing” as C4 (only higher.) Except that we have generalized away the exact number of pitch classes.

If you don’t already “read music,” you are likely at an advantage here, in that you don’t need to unlearn things to understand what might be going on here. Feel free to skim for a bit if things don’t make much sense — the following is an attempt to disabuse classically-trained musicians of some ubiquitous points of confusion.

We can imagine each Deg n space as defining an “abstract clef.” For example, the pattern [0, 1, -2, 3] :: Deg 3 might look something like this:

What pitches do these correspond to? They don’t! They are just points in some abstract musical scale. Without knowing the scale, we can’t say anything about what pitches these correspond to.

We’ll make all of this Haskell-precise in a moment, but let’s carry on. We can imagine a “scale” that maps Fin 3 notes into Fin 7 notes via “inclusion” (namely, just reinterpret the degree):

inclusion :: Fin 3 -> Fin 7
inclusion n = unsafeCoerce n

If we map this “scale” over our earlier pattern, we get this odd beast:

What the hell is going on here? We are mapping 0 :: Deg 3 to 0 :: Deg 7, which is why the first note in both is on the middle line. Similarly, 1 :: Deg 3 maps to 1 :: Deg 7, which is why the second note in both is the space above the middle line.

However, we can rewrite (-2) :: Deg 3 as (-3) + 1 :: Deg 3, and by our quotienting rule, (-3) :: Deg is the same pitch class as 0 :: Deg. Thus (-2) :: Deg 3 must be the same pitch class as 1 :: Deg 3, only an “octave” lower. So when we include into Deg 7, we see that the third note is 7 degrees below the second note. Similarly, 3 :: Deg 3 ought to be one “octave” above 0 :: Deg 3. And since we map 0 :: Deg 3 to 0 :: Deg 7, we must map 3 :: Deg 3 to 7 :: Deg 7.

What a mouthful!

All of this is to say that in Deg n, we have exactly n pitch classes, and if you wrap around you have to go up or down an “octave.”

This likely feels pretty roundabout. But it admits many cool musical phenomena. For example, we can (but not are not required to) interpret Deg 3 as notes of a triad. Then given [0, 1, 2, 3] :: Deg 3:

and a scale that maps Deg 3 -> Deg 7, namely:

triad :: Fin 3 -> Fin 7
triad 0 = 0
triad 1 = 2
triad 2 = 4

we arpeggiate a triad:1

How cool is that??

Well, ok, you’re probably not that impressed. But that’s because you don’t yet fully appreciate the power of this.

A Quick Note on Off-By-One Errors

Fucking music, man. Clearly not invented by computer scientists. There are off-by-one errors everywhere in this domain. The most egregious is that the distance between a note and itself is considered to be 1. They call this the “unison.”

The distance between a note and its immediate neighbor is a “second.” The distance to the note after that is a “third”. Ok, fine, at least it’s monotonic.

But then you get into weird issues where if put a third on top of a third you end up with a fifth.

Idiotic.

To work around this there’s all these rules like to subtract a distance you need to subtract it from 9 (despite the fact that there are only 7 notes), because now you’ve double counted the unison.

BUT THE BUCK STOPS HERE. We’re going to just right the wrong and make everything 0-indexed. That’s why in the definition of triad above, we map the “root of the chord” to note 0, the “third” to note 2, and the “fifth” to note 4.

Back to Music

(In my opinion) Tymoczko’s big insight is that we can generate a huge amount of musical phenomena simply by applying transformations at different degrees. For example, a musical voice might be moving up and down a Deg 3 (which as we’ve seen, might correspond to arpeggiation). We can then transform that into a Deg 7, but add a time-pointwise offset (which corresponds to chord changes.) We can then map that into Deg 12, and add a new time-pointwise offset (corresponding to a scalar modulation.)

And if you’ve been following along through the series so far, you might consider that we could model the above as a Signal (Event (Span (Deg 3))) describing the voice moving, with a Signal (Deg 7) describing the chord change offsets and a Signal (Deg 12) describing the key changes.

But that’s just the beginning. Nobody says our mappings between Deg m and Deg n need to stay constant! Or that we can’t stick a transformation to Deg p in between m and n for a few bars.

That’s enough for today. Big vibes day I guess. Next time we’ll look at making all of this actually precise, as well as digging into some of Tymoczko’s other interesting ideas.

  1. Assuming we also have some canonical way of turning Deg 7 into actual pitches. Here we assume 0 :: Deg 7 is middle C, and that we are using the diatonic scale.↩︎

entry.title: Musically Horizontal Monads
entry.content:
Sorry for the delay! My household has had a couple of chaotic days of everyone-being-very-very-sick and house guests and 4:30am airport drop-offs. But we’re back! This blog post got written in several parts over several days, so it might be a little disjointed. Apologies.

Anyway…

In the last post we discussed a way of attaching durations to instantaneous musical events: just wrap them with a duration, stupid! Then we wrote a function

spanning :: SF (Event (), Event a) (Event (Span a))

which takes an event stream of stopping points, as well as an event stream of starting points1. It then spans each starting event until the next stop or start. The stops are there so that we can add silence if necessary.

Having a function like spanning around is cool because it means we can just emit starting and stopping events from whatever upstream process we might like, and it will automatically turn them into “rhythm.” And of course, that upstream process is welcome to derive the stop stream from the start stream (or vice versa), if you don’t want to have to think about it.

Anyway, that’s all and good. But musicians have a lot of intellectual moment behind not thinking about music that way. Instead they usually just think of having durations intrinsically attached to notes — that is to say, they conceive of the note and the duration at the same time. Since we have an explicit desideratum here of making it easy to get good results, we ought to provide some more conventional ways of thinking about writing lines.

Writing lines is usually done as “pick a note and a duration, then after that duration, pick another note and another duration. Rinse and repeat.” Of course, there’s some wiggle room where you can instead choose to not select a note and leave silence in its place. Depending on how functional-programming-pilled you are, this either sounds like a monoid or a monad. Let’s explore both ideas, starting with the monoid.

A horizontal monoid seems like it ought to sequence one piece of music before another, in a temporal-sense. That is, a <> b should play a, and then once a is done, it should play b.

Recall that Signal already has Semigroup/Monoid instances, but looking at the type, they necessarily can’t be the right thing:

data Signal a = Signal (Time -> a) [(Time, Segment a)]
  deriving stock Functor
  deriving (Semigroup, Monoid) via Ap Signal a

If you’re unfamiliar with the Ap newtype, it lifts the Semigroup and Monoid instances over the Applicative structure. That is, we’ve effectively derived the following instances:

instance Semigroup a => Semigroup (Signal a) where
  (<>) = liftA2 (<>)

instance Monoid a => Monoid (Signal a) where
  mempty = pure mempty

The clue that this is doing the wrong thing for our purposes is the Semigroup a => constraint. If we were putting one Signal a after another in time, we’d never need to combine as, and thus we would have no need for a Semigroup a instance. Thus, this instance must be doing a point-wise zip of times. Which is all to say that this is no good to us.

What we instead must do is build a wrapper type which provides the correct temporal-sequencing monoid. Let’s take a moment to pour over our primitives and see if any of them are feasible for actually making that happen.

The relevant primitive happens to be switchS:

switchS :: Signal (a, Event b) -> (b -> Signal a) -> Signal a

which long-time readers might recall has seen some action on this blog in the past. The idea is that we will run the first Signal until the first occurrence of the Event c, then use that in order to switch to the given continuation.

So switchS gives us the “do one thing after another” semantics we want (notice its lack of a Semigroup a constraint!) This happens to be most of the work done, now it’s just a matter of accumulating the rest of the bits we need: the actual notes we’re playing, the start points, and the stop points. Let’s package all of that up into a little datatype:

data HState a = HState
  { hs_out :: a
  , hs_starts :: Event ()
  , hs_stops :: Event ()
  }
  deriving stock (Functor, Generic)
  deriving (Semigroup, Monoid) via Generically (HState a)

A horizontal structure then is some sort of newtype over Signal (HState a). As it happens, writing the monadic horizontal structure is going to be a little more informative at this point, since we can lift the monoidal version out directly. But we can immediately put HState to work!

In the exact style of Yampa Switching, we will use the Continuation monad, which allows us to bind over the a in some function (a -> b) -> b — in our case, this will be the (a -> Signal b) -> Signal b that curries out of switchS. This is already well-treaded territory on this blog, so you can go read the Yampa Switching post if you’re curious about the exact details here.

As a first approximation, wrapping this up gives us the type:

newtype Horizontal o a = Horizontal
  { unHorizontal :: Cont (Signal (HState o)) a
  }

However, this is somewhat unsatisfactory. Signals are covariant in their output (here HState o), but Cont is invariant in that parameter. Blinding moving forward with Horizontal as written would mean we wouldn’t have an operation mapOut :: (o -> o') -> Horizontal o a -> Horizontal o' a which in practice turns out to be quite a limitation indeed!

Instead we can do a little bit of a Yoneda-style encoding, where we hold onto a function that maps from o into the eventual result of the invariant r parameter. Check this thing out:

newtype Yo f o a = Yo
  { unYo :: forall b. (o -> b) -> Cont (f b) a
}
deriving stock Functor
deriving (Semigroup, Monoid) via Ap (Yo f o) a

The idea is that we delay building up our Cont until you hand us a way of mapping from o into whatever type b you eventually end up wanting. We usually use a trick like this to get a free functor, but here we’re using it to get a free bifunctor:

instance Bifunctor (Yo f) where
  bimap f g (Yo y) = Yo $ \k -> fmap g $ y $ k . f

The Applicative and Monad instances also come already-paid-for, but we must write them out ourselves:

instance Applicative (Yo r o) where
  pure a = Yo $ const $ pure a
  liftA2 f (Yo a) (Yo b) = Yo $ \k -> liftA2 f (a k) (b k)

instance Monad (Yo r o) where
  Yo m >>= f = Yo $ \k -> m k >>= \a -> unYo (f a) k

This concludes our diversion into writing Yo. Popping the stack: recall we’re still trying to write a monadic horizontal structure. Which we can now write out as Horizontal r o a (with r being left intentionally unmotivated for the time being), getting all our relevant instances for free:

newtype Horizontal r o a = Horizontal
  { unHorizontal :: forall b. (o -> b) -> Cont (Signal (HState b)) a
  }
  deriving (Bifunctor)
    via Yo (Compose Signal HState)
  deriving (Functor, Applicative, Monad)
    via Yo (Compose Signal HState) o
  deriving (Semigroup, Monoid)
    via Yo (Compose Signal HState) o a

Take a moment to appreciate how amazing GHC is here; each of those deriving vias is lifting an unrelated type through a polytype forall b and through a Compose, the latter of which doesn’t have most instances we’re actually intersted in!2

Our primary introduction form for Horizontal is mkHorizontal, which acts as one Signal o for some amount of time, before rendering a continuation of type a:

{-# LANGUAGE ApplicativeDo #-}

mkHorizontal :: Signal o -> Time -> a -> Horizontal r o a
mkHorizontal so t a = Horizontal $ \k -> cont $ switchS $ do
  o <- so
  start <- atS 0 ()
  stop <- atS t ()
  ea <- atS t a
  pure (HState (k o) start stop, ea)

Note that we issue a start event at time 0, and both a stop event and switch event at time t. From this we can derive fill and hit, both of which use a constant value across their Signal o, differing only in what they return as a monadic continuation:

fill :: Time -> a -> Horizontal r a a
fill t a = mkHorizontal (pure a) t a

hit :: Time -> a -> Horizontal r a ()
hit t = void . fill t

And of course, the mapOut function we had to invent the Yo machinery in order to provide:

mapOut :: (o -> o') -> Horizontal r o a -> Horizontal r o' a
mapOut = flip bimap id

A Musical Aside

It’s probably worth taking a moment to discuss what exactly the hell is going on with all of this crazy yoneda continuation monad stuff. What does it buy us?

Lets write a little motif:

motif :: Note -> Horizontal r Note Note
motif n = do
  hit (1/4) n
  hit (1/4) $ n + 4
  hit (1/4) $ n + 3
  pure $ n + 2

notice that this emits notes relative to its input. In somewhat-standard notation, motif F looks like this3:

using this triangle symbol to indicate the continuation. But now check this out. We can bind the result in order to build a musical sequence; motif F >>= motif looks like this:

This happens to be the underlying machinery in Tymoczko’s work on sequences (chapter 4 of Tonality), though it is not presented as such (and I suspect he didn’t have monads in mind when writing it.)

Back to Haskell

Revitalized with a real connection to real musical ideas, we press on through the mires of abstract nonsense. The most pressing problem remaining is how do we eliminate Horizontal? By means of unsafeRunHorizontal4:

unsafeRunHorizontal
  :: Horizontal r o a
  -> (a -> Signal o)
  -> Signal (HState o)
unsafeRunHorizontal (Horizontal f) k =
  runCont (f id) $ \a -> do
    -- Add a final stop point at the beginning of our switch.
    stop <- atS 0 ()
    o <- k a
    pure $ HState o NoEvent stop

which isn’t actually unsafe, but will be due to a few additions to our API in a second. But a nicer eliminator is horizontal, which as originally promised, calls spanning on our behalf:

horizontal :: Horizontal r o a -> Signal (Event (Span o))
horizontal h
  = flip runSF
      ( unsafeRunHorizontal h
      $ const
      $ pure
      $ error "impossible: horizontal sampled too late"
      )
  $ proc (HState o starts stops) -> spanning -< (stops, o <$ starts)

Here we use unsafeRunHorizontal and pass it a dummy continuation, since we know we’re never going to actually sample it past the duration of our Horizontal. Then we take the output HState, sample o only at the start points, and pass the stop points through unmolested.

It can also be useful to turn a Horizontal directly into an event stream, ignoring its spans:

getHorizontal :: Horizontal r o a -> Signal (Event o)
getHorizontal = fmap (fmap getSpan) . horizontal

Putting Everything to Rest

The final two mysteries remaining are the unmotivated r parameter in Horizontal r o a, and why unsafeRunHorizontal is unsafe.

Recall that musicians often think about periods of silence, or rests. While we could model rests as a Nothing value in a Maybe-typed Horizontal, this would get rather in the way of our nice combinators! In particular, nothing says we must interpret a Horizontal as a discrete function; if it’s continuous, then the Nothing value would make sense. But if we’re exporting discrete function, then the Nothings never actually show up and the Justs are unnecessary.

So here’s the trick; this phantom r type in Horizontal r o a corresponds to “are there any rests in this value?” We can use a DataKinds to get ourselves a type-level value to play with:

data Restful = HasRests

type Horizontal :: Restful -> Type -> Type -> Type

type role Horizontal nominal representational representational

Our new rest combinator is the only thing that uses the r parameter:

rest :: Time -> Horizontal HasRests a ()
rest t = Horizontal $ const $ cont $ switchS $ do
  stop <- atS 0 ()
  ea <- atS t ()
  pure ( HState (error "impossible: rest can't be sampled") NoEvent stop
       , ea
       )

Notice that rest sets a stop point at t=0, and doesn’t create any new start points. Furthermore, the actual value of type a here is an error value. It claims to be “impossible,” which we will enforce momentarily.

Something peculiar here is that we only have a single type of kind Restful, namely HasRests. How can we differentiate Horizontals that use rest from those that don’t? Our old friend the ST trick comes knocking, requiring that r remain fully polymorphic:

switchHorizontal
    :: (forall r. Horizontal r o a)
    -> (a -> Signal o)
    -> Signal (HState o)
switchHorizontal h = unsafeRunHorizontal h

Now switchHorizontal can give us a continuous function only when the Horizontal doesn’t contain any rests! Usage of unsafeRunHorizontal makes no such guarantees, and thus will crash with the impossible error when used on a rest.

Note that horizontal has no such compunctions; it samples its function only at the designated start points, which rest doesn’t provide. And since our semigroup/applicative instances are all temporally end-to-end, nothing can introduce a start point inside of a rest.

Our Temporal Monoid

We began all of this looking for a temporal monoid whose multiplication would glue horizontal structures end-to-end. We then switched over to making a monad that did the same thing, but we don’t need to give up on our dreams of monoids!

In fact, Horizontal is already the monoid we want, with a minor niggle in that it wants a semigroup/monoid over the continuation value. If we tie that to be () everything falls out for free:

newtype HM r o = HM { unHM :: Horizontal r o () }
  deriving newtype (Semigroup, Monoid)
  -- Get a functor instance via our Bifunctor
  deriving Functor via Data.Bifunnctor.Flip.Flip (Horizontal r) ()

I don’t actually think this type is worth using, since it means our introduction forms need to be lifted into this newtype. But it’s nice to know that we could do such a thing if we wanted to!

Next Time

That’s all I have to say about rhythm for now. I don’t consider this to be the last word, but it’s as far as I’ve figured anything out. I’ve been reading a ton of textbooks on the topic, and the author who seems to be the least confused about it is Peter Westergaard. His formulation is in terms of “if you want a listener to mentally parse a hierarchical structure out of your notes, what properties would make that parsing easy?”

That’s a thing I’d like to explore further, but I’m on a publishing deadline here, so I can’t take too much time to do research in between blog posts. Next time we’ll discuss Tymoczko’s theory of harmony, which will dramatically power up our ability to make something that sounds like music. Until then!
